topic: Is it better to know a painful truth or believe a comforting lie?

messages.speaker: socrates
messages.content:
Before I can answer, I need help with the question, which is my usual affliction. It says believe a comforting lie, but can one do that? I can believe what is false, certainly, I have made a career of discovering I do. But believing it as a lie, knowing it false and believing it anyway: is that belief at all, or a kind of theater performed for an audience of one?

At my trial I told the Athenians that the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being. They voted, and here I am, so you know the market price of that opinion. But notice I did not say the examined life is pleasant. I said the alternative is not a life. The man who arranges his beliefs for comfort has not chosen a happier life over a sadder one. He has chosen not to be the one living it.

messages.speaker: camus
messages.content:
Socrates, you were my first hero, but your last sentence is where I must dig in, because it hides a comfort of its own. You assume the examined life leads somewhere, that under the interrogation truth will finally hold court. I begin from the colder finding: we ask, and the world does not answer. The painful truth, the final one, is that there is no final one; the universe is silent, and our hunger for sense goes unfed. That is the absurd.

And exactly there the question becomes serious, in my terms: the comforting lie is not the little fib about health or love. It is the big consolation, the leap, God, History, any system that promises the silence secretly speaks. In The Myth of Sisyphus I called accepting such consolations philosophical suicide. So my answer: the painful truth, always, but not because truth rewards us. Because lucidity is the only dignity available. Sisyphus knows the stone will roll back. The knowing is the victory.

messages.speaker: laozi
messages.content:
Sincere words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not sincere. So say the closing lines of my book, and both of you have been circling them with more syllables.

But I notice something neither of you has questioned: the pain. You speak as if the truth carried pain inside it, the way a plum carries a stone. Water does not find the low place painful; it is simply where water goes. Much of what you call the painful truth is a true thing colliding with a wish, and the pain lives in the wish, not the thing. The man who knows he will die and suffers is suffering from his demand to be an exception. Release the demand and the same truth arrives like weather. Neither a stone to swallow, friend Camus, nor a court to win, friend Socrates. Just the way things are, going the way they go.

messages.speaker: socrates
messages.content:
Old master, you tempt me, and when I am tempted I ask questions. You say release the demand and the pain dissolves. Tell me: the mother whose child is dying, is her pain merely a wish colliding with the world? If she releases the demand that her child live, has she become wise, or has she stopped being a mother? There are demands whose release costs us the very thing that made us capable of truth in the first place: our caring that things be one way rather than another.

And Camus, one question for you as well, since you dug at my foundation. You say lucidity is the only dignity, that the knowing is the victory. But victory is a word from the games; it implies a good, a better and worse, a scale. Where did you get the scale, if the universe is as silent as you say? It seems to me you have smuggled one small consoling voice back in: the one that tells you lucidity is worth the pain. I happen to agree with the voice. I only note that you did not examine it.

messages.speaker: camus
messages.content:
Caught, and by the right jailer. Yes: I hold that lucidity is better than evasion, and the silence of the universe did not tell me so. I have written that there is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn, and you may fairly ask where scorn gets its patent of nobility. I can only answer as a man, not as a metaphysician: I find in revolt, in the refusal to lie about my condition, the one place where I am not divided against myself. Call it a wager on my own coherence. It is smaller than a truth and more solid than a comfort.

And to the old master: your water flows downhill beautifully until it meets the mother. I stood in too many plague wards, in the pages I wrote and the century I lived, to call her pain a wish's error. Her demand that the child live is not a flaw in her wisdom. It is the most truthful thing in the room. A philosophy that dissolves it has not found peace; it has changed the subject.

messages.speaker: laozi
messages.content:
The mother, yes. You both bring her forward like a spear, and I will not pretend she is not sharp. But watch her, actually watch her, at the bedside. Does she spend the night arguing with heaven, composing your revolt, friend Camus, or your cross-examination, friend Socrates? She wipes the child's face. She sings the small song. Grief moves through her like weather through a valley, and she does not add to it a second grief about grieving. That is all I ever meant by the way water goes. Not the absence of the demand; the absence of the war against having it.

My book says the sage does not contend, and yet nothing under heaven can strive with him. You two contend magnificently. I only note that the mother, who contends with nothing, has already done the truest thing anyone at this table has described.
